clue.text: Mature spirit in the money, in low spirits, however

indicators.note: the drink and the age word sit inside the cash letters, as the clue's 'in the money' puts them

parts.note: d and s are the old British pence and shillings, as in the £sd of pre-decimal money
mature wine or cheese is old
rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A man flush with cash and aged rum is still gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: D and S are the pence and shilling of Britain's pre-1971 money. 'in' puts OLD RUM between them; 'in the doldrums' is to be in low spirits, so 'however' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'in the doldrums' means feeling dejected, so the noun names a state of gloom.

clue.text: "Though an angel should write, still 'tis must print" (Thomas Moore)

definitions.text: "Though an angel should write, still 'tis must print" (Thomas Moore)

parts.words: "Though an angel should write, still 'tis must print" (Thomas Moore)
parts.note: a quotation with its missing word left out; printers' apprentices were nicknamed after imps of hell, so even an angel's writing is printed by them

explanation.surface: A line of verse by the Irish poet Thomas Moore with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A printer's devil was the errand boy of a printing shop; Moore's joke sets angels writing against devils printing.
explanation.definitionFit: A printer's apprentice was traditionally called a printer's devil, the fiends who set an author's words in type.

clue.text: On the side of a delayed mass-meeting ?

parts.note: something delayed arrives late
a rally is a large public gathering

explanation.surface: A protest gathering that started behind schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral means to do with the side, so the adverb means sideways or on the side.

clue.text: Used for setting water-waves ?

explanation.surface: Something that shapes the sea's swell, as a hairdresser shapes curls.
explanation.walkthrough: Hair is set on curlers called rollers; long swelling ocean waves are also rollers.
explanation.definitionFit: Curlers for setting hair are rollers, and large breakers rolling in from the ocean bear the same name.

clue.text: See 5
A secret life was his, in daydreams

definitions.text: A secret life was his, in daydreams

parts.words: A secret life was his, in daydreams
parts.note: points to the James Thurber story about a timid man whose imagined heroics make up a secret life

explanation.surface: A man lives a hidden, heroic existence only in his own fantasies.
explanation.walkthrough: Thurber's 1939 story 'The Secret Life of …' gives its hero's name; the answer runs from 5 across into 4 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Thurber's fantasist hero lives his adventures only in reverie, and his name is now a byword for any daydreamer.

clue.text: Attack as in two directions last month

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word is written both forwards and then backwards, going two ways

parts.note: the same little word is read a second time
ult., short for ultimo, is the formal letter-writer's way of saying last month

explanation.surface: An assault on the attackers was made from both flanks last month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in two directions' means AS is written forwards then backwards, giving ASSA; ULT (ultimo, last month in old business letters) completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: To assault someone is to set upon them violently, a synonym of the verb or noun.

clue.text: Dickensian dance ?

explanation.surface: A dance step drawn from the pages of Charles Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist is Dickens's orphan hero; the twist is also a dance (here older senses of the word as a turn in a dance).
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver's surname in the Dickens novel, and a dance of twisting hips and turns.

clue.text: Again classified the letters RED to RES

explanation.surface: A typesetter re-sorting letters in a word to change its spelling.
explanation.walkthrough: In printing, single pieces of type are 'sorts'; changing the D of RED for an S means the type has been sorted again.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort again is to classify a second time; and swapping a piece of type changes the letters set, a re-sorting of the type sorts.

clue.text: He failed to do his homework for the Danish lesson

definitions.text: He failed to do his homework for the Danish lesson

parts.words: He failed to do his homework for the Danish lesson
parts.note: describes the English king nicknamed 'the Unready', who was unprepared for the Viking invasions, as a schoolboy with no homework done

explanation.surface: A schoolboy turns up to his Danish class unprepared.
explanation.walkthrough: The Anglo-Saxon king nicknamed the Unready (from Old English 'unraed', ill-advised) lost England to the Danish king Sweyn in 1013.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon king known as 'the Unready' was famously ill-prepared for Danish raiders.

clue.text: But such figures would not suggest beauty of form to Malthus

definitions.text: But such figures would not suggest beauty of form to Malthus

parts.words: But such figures would not suggest beauty of form to Malthus
parts.note: the phrase for a woman's bust, waist and hip measurements also means births and deaths data, which the population economist Malthus studied

explanation.surface: An economist sees only population tables where others see a shapely figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means a woman's measurements, but its original sense is records of births, deaths and marriages, the material of Thomas Malthus's population theory.
explanation.definitionFit: Data on births, marriages and deaths are this phrase in demography, and it is also slang for bust, waist and hip measurements.

clue.text: It was grand to take more than a shilling

definitions.text: It was grand to take more than a shilling

parts.words: It was grand to take more than a shilling
parts.note: old English law called theft of goods worth over twelve pence the grand form of the crime

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it splendid to pocket over a shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: Until 1827 English law split theft into petty and grand, the line being twelve pence, one shilling (a pre-decimal British coin).
explanation.definitionFit: Theft is the plain synonym; grand theft was the legal name for stealing goods above a shilling's value.

clue.text: Great Circle Line

parts.note: suggests a London Underground route, but describes the one parallel of latitude that is a great circle round the globe

explanation.surface: A grand name for a railway route that goes round in a loop.
explanation.walkthrough: London's Circle Line is an Underground route; a great circle is one dividing the globe into equal halves, and only one line of latitude is one.
explanation.definitionFit: The imaginary line midway between the poles is the only parallel of latitude that is a great circle.

clue.text: A swan-song from a Scotsman ?

parts.note: a swan's song is the last air it sings before dying

explanation.surface: A Highlander sings his final farewell song.
explanation.walkthrough: Swans were said to sing once, just before death, so a swan-song is a last air.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish form of the given name Alexander, so one man bearing it stands for a Scot.

clue.text: He keeps fishes-of one who precedes them ?

explanation.surface: A fish-keeper described in astrological terms.
explanation.walkthrough: One keeping an aquarium is an aquarian; Aquarius is the sign of the zodiac just before Pisces, the Fishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a fish tank, and someone born under the Water Carrier, the star sign that comes right before Pisces.

clue.text: Soprano's notes put an Englishman, but not mad dogs, in the shade

definitions.text: put an Englishman, but not mad dogs, in the shade

parts.note: the soprano sings the top line of a choir
E is a musical note, here two of them

explanation.surface: A singer's high notes and Noel Coward's song about mad dogs and Englishmen in the midday sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward's song says only mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun; the Englishman's sun helmet shades him, the dogs have none.
explanation.definitionFit: A pith helmet worn by colonial Britons to keep the tropical sun off their heads.

clue.text: Food legally established in Scotland by the German

parts.note: Scots law keeps the verdicts 'proven' and 'not proven'
der is a German word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A dish proven acceptable by a Scottish court and a German.
explanation.walkthrough: Scots criminal courts can return 'not proven', so the past participle is the Scottish legal form.
explanation.definitionFit: Provisions or fodder, an old word for food and especially animal feed.

clue.text: A casual caller, this bird ?

parts.note: a visitor who drops by is said to pop in, and a jay is a bird, so the bird is described as a jay that pops in

explanation.surface: A bird that drops in on its neighbours without invitation.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as POP IN + JAY, a jay making a casual visit; the whole word is an old name for a parrot, and for a vain dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic name for a parrot, a showy bird, which by extension also means a conceited fop.

clue.text: Reichenbach's force confuses Doyle

indicators.note: the author's surname is confused, mixing up its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A detective writer's name is muddled with the Reichenbach Falls, where Holmes 'died'.
explanation.walkthrough: Sherlock Holmes went over the Reichenbach Falls in Doyle's story; Baron von Reichenbach was a chemist who named a supposed natural force.
explanation.definitionFit: Baron von Reichenbach's name for a supposed vital energy pervading nature, linked with magnetism.

clue.text: Involve little brother in fruit-raising

indicators.note: the sibling is placed inside the turned-up fruit word
in a down clue raising a word lifts it, reading it bottom to top

parts.note: a lime is a citrus fruit
bro is a short form of brother

explanation.surface: A small boy is drawn into fruit growing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns LIME upwards to EMIL in this down clue, and 'in' sets BRO inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To embroil someone is to entangle or drag them into a dispute, a synonym of involve.

clue.text: The silly nut rowed without regard for this current !

indicators.note: a silly nut makes these words a muddled, foolish arrangement of letters

explanation.surface: A foolish oarsman ignores the dangerous current pulling under his boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' shuffles NUT ROWED; the rower's neglect of the current paints the scene of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A current beneath the surface flowing against the waves on top, as near a beach.

clue.text: Role Jack's taken up as vermin-destroyer

indicators.note: in a down entry taking words up writes them from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a part is a role in a play
Jack and tar are both old names for a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor takes on the job of pest controller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' turns the whole run PARTTAR upwards, giving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A device for catching vermin, such as rodents, destroys them.

clue.text: Plague a beginner to get a nap?

parts.note: to plague is to tease or harass
L for learner, the L-plate of British beginner drivers

explanation.surface: Pestering a newcomer until they want a snooze.
explanation.walkthrough: A nap here is the raised fibres of cloth, not a sleep; teasel heads were used to raise it. L is from the L-plate a British learner driver displays.
explanation.definitionFit: A prickly plant whose dried heads were used to brush up the fibres on woollen cloth.

clue.text: He has central protection against spilling his drink

definitions.text: He has central protection against spilling his drink

parts.words: He has central protection against spilling his drink
parts.note: the drinker's name holds a bib, a guard against spills, right in its middle

explanation.surface: A drinker wears a bib to save his shirt from his spilled glass.
explanation.walkthrough: A bib protects against spills, and the three letters BIB stand at the centre of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: One who drinks, especially alcohol, which fits a man protecting himself from spilt drink.

clue.text: Berry calls a cab back, reverses the account

indicators.note: a cab called back is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the account's abbreviation is turned the other way round

parts.note: a/c is the common abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: Someone hails a taxi to return and cancels the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns CAB to BAC and 'reverses' turns AC (a/c, account) to CA.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacca is the botanical Latin for a berry, a fleshy fruit with seeds.

clue.text: It's animal — or mineral, on reflection

definitions.text: It's animal — or mineral, on reflection

parts.words: It's animal — or mineral, on reflection
parts.note: suggests the parlour game Animal, Vegetable or Mineral: a pet's organ, a gemstone, and a road stud that shines back in headlights

explanation.surface: A guessing game: is the thing animal, vegetable or mineral?
explanation.walkthrough: The term is an animal's eye, a chatoyant gemstone, and the reflecting studs in British road centre lines that glint in headlights.
explanation.definitionFit: A gem with a shifting band of light, a feline organ, and a reflector on roads all share the name.

clue.text: There's nothing to follow a small chamber music maker

indicators.note: the zero word comes after the room word, following it

parts.note: a cell is a small room, as in a prison or monastery
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A small chamber orchestra has nothing to play after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' puts O after CELL. The surface's chamber music is a red herring: the chamber is a cell.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowed string instrument, an instrument being something that makes music.

clue.text: He'll never get his master's ticket !

definitions.text: He'll never get his master's ticket !

parts.words: He'll never get his master's ticket !
parts.note: a ship's master needs a certificate, but the proverb says this dabbler in every craft is master of none

explanation.surface: A sailor who will never qualify as a ship's captain.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb ends '… master of none'; a master's ticket is the certificate to captain a merchant ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial dabbler has many skills but masters none, so never qualifies as master of any.

clue.text: Youth leader in good time annually

indicators.note: the leader of the word is its opening letter

parts.note: arriving in good time means arriving early

explanation.surface: The head of a youth club turns up early every year.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done once each year happens annually.

clue.text: Napoleon's Violet

parts.note: his supporters toasted the exiled emperor as 'Caporal la Violette', the military rank plus the flower he promised to return with in spring

explanation.surface: The French emperor's favourite flower.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon was the 'Little Corporal' to his troops, and in exile on Elba he was toasted as Corporal Violet, the violet being his emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: The army rank Napoleon was nicknamed by, half of his Bonapartist codename 'Corporal Violet'.
